title: Draupadi's sari

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dice, and a wise man who staked everything, one throw at a time. Nobody stopped the hand.

Draupadi isn't even in the hall. She's in the women's rooms when a servant comes to tell her she's been lost in a game she wasn't playing: she now belongs to the Kauravas, and must come. Instead of coming, she sends back a question. It's a sharp question, and nobody in that hall, not the kings, not the elders, can answer it. This is a hard scene, about a woman humiliated in public, so i'll tell it carefully.
screen: `LOST IN A GAME SHE WASN'T PLAYING.` → `SHE SENDS BACK A QUESTION.` → `A HARD SCENE, TOLD CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Her question: when Yudhishthira staked me, had he already lost himself? If he had, he was a slave, and what right does a slave have to stake anyone? Duryodhana doesn't answer. He sends his brother Dushasana, who drags her into the hall by her hair. Before the whole court, Draupadi asks again. The grandfather Bhishma, the elder everyone looks to, says the ways of dharma are subtle, and he can't say. Only one of the hundred Kaurava brothers, the young Vikarna, stands up and says she's right, and he's shouted down. Then the worst moment. Dushasana is ordered to strip her, in front of everyone. He grabs the end of her garment and pulls. And pulls. The cloth keeps coming, yard after yard, a mountain of it piling up on the floor, until Dushasana collapses, exhausted, and Draupadi is still standing, still covered. In the popular telling, she has called on Krishna, and he answers her with cloth that never ends. Tellings differ on how much they say about how it happens, but in each of them the cloth doesn't end. Either way, the one who was supposed to be shamed is the one left standing, and the hall knows it. Bhima swears a terrible vow of revenge. Jackals howl, a bad omen. The blind king, frightened, finally offers Draupadi wishes, and she uses them to free her husbands. Her question was never answered. Her dignity was never removed.
screen: `HAD HE ALREADY LOST HIMSELF?` · `THE ELDERS CAN'T ANSWER.` · `THE CLOTH KEEPS COMING.` · `SHE'S THE ONE LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: Sit with your spine straight, the way Draupadi stood, and remember a time someone tried to shame you: a teacher, a boss, a relative, a crowd online. Notice that you're still here; whatever they took, they didn't get all of you. Then picture someone being shamed right now, in your world or in the news, covered, protected, still standing, and if you pray, hold them there.
Draupadi's sari. The cloth that wouldn't end, and a question the whole court couldn't answer.
Your line: unending. Her question still hangs there in that hall, unanswered. That's day seventy-three.

howItsDone: Draupadi's disrobing and the unending cloth are retold again and again in dance, theater and devotional song; devotees see in it Krishna's protection of those who call on him, and in parts of south India Draupadi herself is worshiped as a goddess.

original.note: Sanskrit: Draupadi, 'daughter of Drupada', the king of Panchala.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic sari.
what it means: a woman humiliated in public asks a question no one can answer, and the one meant to be shamed is left standing.
what a scholar hears: in the Pune critical edition the cloth still multiplies, but her call to Krishna is in the later manuscripts, not the main text.

notes: Critical edition: the writer's understanding is that the Pune critical edition keeps the multiplying cloth but relegates Draupadi's explicit invocation of Krishna to the appendix. Please confirm before the trapdoor ships.

Bhima's vow (to drink Dushasana's blood and break Duryodhana's thigh) is only called 'a terrible vow of revenge'; Draupadi's vow to leave her hair unbound is left for later.
